title: Incorporating Societal Context
subtitle: Make the people, assumptions, and feedback around software visible
summary: Pip draws a benefits portal as inputs and outputs. Residents and caseworkers add documents, transport, institutions, beliefs, and changing practices: the surrounding social system matters. Agents, precepts, and artifacts make those forces visible. Explicit causal assumptions and loops show how an intervention might change later behavior and data. The book’s health-care example warns that a convenient proxy can misrepresent need; its toxicity-classification case shows the value of specialists and constructive criticism. Pip treats the model as revisable evidence for discussion, not a complete description of society.

concepts.title: Societal context
concepts.body: Pip draws the benefits portal as one form and one decision. Residents add missing pieces: access to documents, caseworker practices, local institutions, and physical infrastructure. Societal context is a changing complex system around the software. Its agents include people and institutions, its precepts include their beliefs, and its artifacts include interfaces, datasets, laws, and infrastructure. The submission alone cannot explain the outcome.

steps.text: Pip expands the initial input-output sketch.
The interface is one artifact, not the whole system.
Beliefs and infrastructure change the outcomes around the software.

concepts.title: Agents, precepts, artifacts
concepts.body: The speech-coaching review begins with microphones. Pip asks who else belongs on the map. In SpeekSplendid, speech-impaired users and coaches are agents; beliefs about “good” speech and language norms are precepts; microphones and accessibility rules are artifacts. A tutoring example has learners, teachers, and lesson materials too. Naming the categories keeps an abstract model from erasing whose assumptions shape the service.

steps.text: Pip names what the abstract model might otherwise hide.
Microphones, rules, and interfaces are artifacts affecting the service.

concepts.title: Explicit causality
concepts.body: Pip expects appointment reminders to improve attendance. A resident asks, “Will the ferry arrive?” The assumed cause is now visible: a reminder may change behavior only when constraints permit it. Abstraction helps reasoning, but hidden assumptions distort it. Pip writes the causal relationship down so others can challenge it, including how changed access or behavior might alter data used in later decisions.

steps.text: Pip states a causal assumption explicitly.
Test the relationship instead of treating it as a guaranteed effect.

concepts.title: Causal loops
concepts.body: Popular creators get more exposure, then more clicks, then a higher ranking. Pip draws the loop before treating clicks as independent proof of quality. Causal loop diagrams make reinforcing and balancing feedback discussable instead of showing only a one-way pipeline. The team can seek other perspectives, choose knowledgeable collaborators, and test assumptions. A loop suggests where an intervention might create another effect; it does not prove the prediction.

steps.text: Pip asks whether the evidence is feeding back on itself.
Exposure increases the chance of clicks.
Higher ranking increases exposure: a reinforcing loop to investigate.

misconceptions.claim: Societal context is equivalent to ordinary functional correctness.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter separates this concern from “works as coded”: Societal context is a dynamic complex system surrounding software.

misconceptions.claim: A single review proves the product will remain responsible.
misconceptions.correction: Users, contexts, and dependencies change; feedback, monitoring, and revision are required.

scenario.title: Causal map for speech coaching
scenario.context: Pip joins the SpeekSplendid speech-coaching review. Should the team model users, institutions, beliefs, and artifacts before launch, or only the speech signal?

options.label: Build a causal loop with affected experts
options.benefit: Affected experts can challenge assumptions about coaching and feedback.
options.cost: Workshops take time, and diagrams still simplify social complexity.
options.consequence: A speech-impaired participant identifies a harmful proxy. Pip helps the team revise the evaluation plan with that evidence.

options.label: Model only the speech signal
options.benefit: The prototype remains small and technically legible.
options.cost: Institutional context and social feedback stay outside the model.
options.consequence: A narrow accent becomes the prototype’s success measure. Pip’s team learns about the missing perspective through user abandonment.

scenario.debrief: The map does not replace expertise. Pip uses it to expose assumptions and invite the people who can challenge them.

quiz.question: What are the three parts of societal context?
quiz.explanation: The chapter defines agents, beliefs or precepts, and artifacts such as laws, interfaces, or infrastructure.

quiz.question: What does a causal loop diagram add?
options: It proves a prediction will occur.
It makes feedback assumptions and reinforcing or balancing effects discussable.
It removes the need for domain experts.
quiz.explanation: Diagrams expose assumptions and help teams seek other perspectives; they are not proof.

quiz.question: In the SpeekSplendid example, why identify speech-impaired users and language experts?
options: Their context can change what good speech and useful coaching mean.
They provide a replacement for all testing.
quiz.explanation: Different agents and expertise shape the system’s meaning and consequences.
